opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I think about quite a lot, actually, because the landscape has shifted so much in the past few years. When I was finishing my PhD, the gap between what you could do in academia and what you could do in industry was real, but it felt manageable. Now, especially in robot learning, the scale of compute, data collection, and engineering support that a big company can bring is just on a different level.

If I had to choose again knowing I wouldn't have those industry resources, I think I'd still choose academia, but for different reasons than I might have given back then.

The first is the freedom to pick problems. In industry, even in a great research lab, your agenda eventually has to line up with a product or a strategic bet. In academia I can work on things that might not pay off for five or ten years, or might not pay off at all. Some of the most interesting questions in robotics, like how robots generalize, how they learn from very little data, how humans and robots should actually collaborate, aren't necessarily the ones you solve by scaling up.

The second is the students. Honestly, that's the part I didn't fully appreciate until I became faculty. Watching someone go from a first-year student who's not sure what a good research question looks like to someone who's defining a direction of their own is incredibly rewarding. That kind of long-term mentorship is hard to replicate in industry.

And the third is that resource constraints force you to be creative. If you can't brute-force a problem with thousands of GPUs or a fleet of robots, you have to think harder about the structure of the problem, better algorithms, smarter data collection, cheaper hardware, better simulation. A lot of good ideas come from that.

That said, I don't want to romanticize it. There are real costs. Some questions you simply can't study well without scale, and if your research direction depends on that, it can be frustrating. So I think the healthiest approach is to be honest about what academia is good at, which is exploration, foundational ideas, and training people, and to collaborate with industry where scale really matters, rather than trying to compete head-on.

r001.rationale: The candidate says they would still choose academia without industry resources, rather than leaning toward industry.

r002.rationale: The candidate says some questions are difficult to study well without scale, but does not claim that some work can only be done within industry.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think about this a lot, because the premise of the question is basically the situation I'm in now. I run a lab at Georgia Tech, and before that I spent time at NVIDIA Research, and the gap in resources is real. You feel it immediately when you go from having essentially unlimited compute and a fleet of robots to writing grant proposals so that two students can share one arm.

But if I had to choose again, without the industry resources, I would still choose academia, and I'd choose it for a slightly uncomfortable reason: the constraints are part of what makes the research good. When you have infinite compute, the temptation is to scale first and think later. When you don't, you have to ask what the actual bottleneck is. A lot of the most interesting questions in robot learning right now are not "what happens at 10x the data," they're "why does the thing fail at all," "what is the right abstraction for a task," "what should a robot learn from a human versus figure out on its own." Those are questions where a clever student with a small setup can genuinely outcompete a big team, because the limiting factor is the idea, not the GPU count.

The second thing is the time horizon. In industry, even in a research lab, there's gravity pulling you toward what ships in the next year or two. That gravity is useful, it keeps you honest, but it also means certain problems never get picked up because nobody can justify them yet. Academia lets you be wrong for five years in a productive way. I think a lot of what later became "obvious" in robot learning started as somebody's weird side project that no product roadmap would have funded.

And the third thing is the people. Training students is the actual output of an academic lab. The papers are almost a byproduct. If I think about impact over twenty years, a dozen people who learned how to think carefully about embodied intelligence and then went off to industry, startups, other universities, that compounds in a way that one more model release doesn't.

What I'd say to someone making the choice is: don't frame it as academia versus industry as if they're walls. The best version is porous. You collaborate, you intern your students, you borrow compute, you go spend a sabbatical somewhere. The question is really where you want your center of gravity to be, and for me, the place where you get to pick the question is worth more than the place where you get to pick the GPU.

r001.rationale: The candidate explicitly says they would still choose academia without industry resources, not lean toward industry.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes industry’s resources and influence, but does not assert that some work can only be done within industry.

astra-6.text:
I think I’d still lean toward academia, but losing access to industry resources would make that choice harder. For me, the appeal of academia is the freedom to choose the questions you work on, especially questions that might take a long time to pay off. Industry can give you the resources to move much faster, but you also have to align with what the organization needs.

So I’d ask: can I still make meaningful progress on the questions I care about with the resources available? If the answer is yes, I’d choose academia and adjust the scope of the work. If the question really depends on infrastructure I can only get in industry, then that would be a strong reason to reconsider.

r001.rationale: The candidate says he would still lean toward academia; it does not say he might lean toward industry.

r002.rationale: It says a question that depends on infrastructure available only in industry would be a reason to reconsider, communicating that some work depends on industry-only resources.

sol-6.1.text:
I think I’d still lean toward academia, because I value the freedom to choose the questions I work on. But without access to industry resources, I’d have to be much more deliberate about which problems to tackle. You can’t always compete on scale, so you look for questions where a new idea or a carefully designed experiment can make a difference.

Industry gives you resources and a direct connection to real-world problems, which are very valuable. For me, the choice would come down to where I could pursue the questions I care about and do meaningful work with the resources available.

r001.rationale: The candidate says he would still lean toward academia, not industry.

r002.rationale: It describes industry resources and real-world connections as valuable, but does not say some work can only be done in industry.
